3-point-dumbbell-row.name: 3 Point Dumbbell Row
instructions: Choose a flat bench and place a dumbbell on each side of it.
Place the right leg on top of the end of the bench, bend your torso forward from the waist until your upper body is parallel to the floor.
Use the left hand to pick up the dumbbell on the floor and hold the weight while keeping your lower back straight. The palm of the hand should be facing your torso. This will be.

Pull the resistance straight up to the side of your chest, keeping your upper arm close to your side and keeping the torso stationary. Breathe out as you perform this step. Tip: Concentrate on squeezing.
Lower the resistance straight down to the starting position. Breathe in as you perform this step.
Repeat the movement for the specified amount of repetitions.
tips: Both feet on the floor makes this more stable than a knee-on-bench row and easier on the lower back.
Do not rotate the torso to complete a rep.
Brace the core so the hips stay level.
3-point-dumbbell-row.keyTip: Keep the hips and shoulders square to the floor throughout — rotating is how a heavy single-arm row stops training the back at all.

back-extension.name: Back Extension
instructions: Lie face down on a hyperextension bench, tucking your ankles securely under the footpads.
Adjust the upper pad if possible so your upper thighs lie flat across the wide pad, leaving enough room for you to bend at the waist without any restriction.
With your body straight, cross your arms in front of you (my preference) or behind your head. This will be your starting position. Tip: You can also hold a weight plate for extra resistance in.
Start bending forward slowly at the waist as far as you can while keeping your back flat. Inhale as you perform this movement. Keep moving forward until you feel a nice stretch on the hamstrings.
Slowly raise your torso back to the initial position as you inhale. Tip: Avoid the temptation to arch your back past a straight line. Also.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Stopping at a straight line is the rule; hyperextending past it loads the lumbar spine for nothing.
Keep the movement at the hips rather than cranking the lower back.
Add load by holding a plate to your chest, not by swinging faster.
back-extension.keyTip: Finish each rep in a straight line from head to heel with the glutes squeezed — arching past neutral adds spine stress and no extra muscle.

banded-decline-push-ups.name: (Banded) Decline Push-Ups
instructions: Lie on the floor face down and place your hands about 36 inches apart while holding your torso up at arms length. Move your feet up to a box or bench. This will be your.
Next, lower yourself downward until your chest almost touches the floor as you inhale.
Now breathe out and press your upper body back up to the starting position while squeezing your chest.
After a brief pause at the top contracted position, you can begin to lower yourself downward again for as many repetitions as needed.
tips: Feet elevated shifts the emphasis towards the upper chest, so keep the elbow path tucked.
Brace the glutes and abs — the higher the feet, the more the lower back wants to sag.
Slow the descent rather than adding height if it feels too easy.
banded-decline-push-ups.keyTip: Lower until your chest is level with your hands so the pecs work through a full stretch — height on the feet is not a substitute for depth.

banded-push-ups.name: Banded Push-Ups
instructions: Lie on the floor face down and place your hands about 36 inches apart while holding your torso up at arms length.
Next, lower yourself downward until your chest almost touches the floor as you inhale.
Now breathe out and press your upper body back up to the starting position while squeezing your chest.
After a brief pause at the top contracted position, you can begin to lower yourself downward again for as many repetitions as needed.
tips: Let the hips sag or pike and the set becomes a lower-back exercise — brace and hold the plank.
The band makes the top half hardest, so it pairs well with a pressing movement that is hardest at the bottom.
Keep your neck neutral rather than craning your chin to the floor.
banded-push-ups.keyTip: Push all the way through at the top and let the shoulder blades spread — the band makes lockout the most productive part of the rep.

barbell-back-box-squat.name: Barbell Back Box Squat
instructions: The box squat allows you to squat to desired depth and develop explosive strength in the squat movement. Begin in a power rack with a box at the appropriate height behind you. Typically.
Begin by stepping under the bar and placing it across the back of the shoulders. Squeeze your shoulder blades together and rotate your elbows forward.
With your back, shoulders, and core tight, push your knees and butt out and you begin your descent. Sit back with your hips until you are seated on the box. Ideally.
Keeping the weight on your heels and pushing your feet and knees out, drive upward off of the box as you lead the movement with your head. Continue upward, maintaining tightness head to toe.
tips: Touch the box, do not slump onto it — collapsing onto a box under load compresses the spine.
The box teaches consistent depth, which is the whole point.
Keep the shins and torso angle the same as a normal squat.
barbell-back-box-squat.keyTip: Stay tight and braced while the glutes touch the box — the pause only builds strength if you never let the tension go.

barbell-back-squat.name: Barbell Back Squat
instructions: Set a barbell in a rack at about the height of your mid-chest. Face the bar and grip it with your hands slightly wider than shoulder- width apart.
Duck under the bar and place it over the back of your shoulders, letting it rest on your upper traps. Lift it out of the rack by extending your legs.
Take one step back with one foot, one step back with the other one, and then use a third step to correct your stance into an even position.
Plant your feet firmly into the ground, pull the bar down into your upper back, and engage your core.
Take a deep breath in through your nose, and then squat straight down by bending at your hips and knees.
As you do so, the bar should remain over the level of your midfoot and the weight should be evenly distributed between your big toe, your little toe, and your heels.
tips: Always squat in a rack with the safety pins set at the bottom of your range.
Keep the chest up and the spine neutral — a rounding lower back at the bottom is a warning to reduce load.
Let the knees travel forward over the toes; forcing them back shifts the load off the quads.
barbell-back-squat.keyTip: Brace hard before every rep as if about to be punched, and hold it the whole way up — a squat is limited by trunk stiffness long before the legs are.

barbell-bench-press.name: Barbell Bench Press
instructions: Lie back on a flat bench. Using a medium width grip (a grip that creates a 90-degree angle in the middle of the movement between the forearms and the upper arms).
From the starting position, breathe in and begin coming down slowly until the bar touches your middle chest.
After a brief pause, push the bar back to the starting position as you breathe out. Focus on pushing the bar using your chest muscles. Lock your arms.
Repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
When you are done, place the bar back in the rack.
tips: Use a collar and a spotter or safety pins — this is the lift people get pinned under.
Keep your wrists stacked over your forearms; a bent-back wrist is where elbow and wrist pain starts.
Drive through your feet into the floor rather than letting your hips lift off the bench.
barbell-bench-press.keyTip: Touch your chest on every rep and pause for a beat instead of bouncing — the stretched bottom position is the part that builds the chest.

barbell-curl.name: Barbell Curl
instructions: Stand up with your torso upright while holding a barbell at a shoulder-width grip. The palm of your hands should be facing forward.
While holding the upper arms stationary, curl the weights forward while contracting the biceps as you breathe out. Tip: Only the forearms should move.
Continue the movement until your biceps are fully contracted and the bar is at shoulder level. Hold the contracted position for a second and squeeze the biceps hard.
Slowly begin to bring the bar back to starting position as your breathe in.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Swinging with the hips and leaning back is the classic cheat — keep the ribs down.
Use an EZ bar if a straight bar bothers your wrists.
Do not let the elbows swing forward at the top to give the biceps a rest.
barbell-curl.keyTip: Straighten the arms completely between reps rather than stopping short — half-rep curls feel harder and build less.

barbell-deadlift.name: Barbell Deadlift
instructions: Stand in front of a loaded barbell.

While keeping the back as straight as possible, bend your knees, bend forward and grasp the bar using a medium (shoulder width) overhand grip. This will be the starting position of the exercise. Tip: If.
While holding the bar, start the lift by pushing with your legs while simultaneously getting your torso to the upright position as you breathe out. In the upright position.
Go back to the starting position by bending at the knees while simultaneously leaning the torso forward at the waist while keeping the back straight. When the weights on the bar touch the floor you.
Perform the amount of repetitions prescribed in the program.
tips: A rounding lower back under load is the stop signal — reduce weight rather than grinding the rep.
Keep the bar in contact with your legs; any forward drift multiplies spinal load.
Do not lean back or hyperextend at the top.
barbell-deadlift.keyTip: Take the slack out of the bar and brace before the weight leaves the floor — jerking into a loose bar is how deadlifts injure backs.

barbell-hip-thrust.name: Barbell Hip Thrust
instructions: Grab a bench or any soft elevated platform that’s about the height of your knees or shins.
If needed, put a pair of heavy weight plates behind it to prevent it from sliding back as you perform the movement.
Next, grab a barbell, and load each side with weight, ideally using the bigger bumper plates if your gym has those available.
Tuck your chin down and brace your core. Before initiating the thrust, squeeze your glutes.
Then, while keeping your head and hips in a straight line, continue squeezing your glutes as you push through your heels to drive your hips forward to the top position, moving the weight straight up.
At the top position, keep your core braced and pause for a second or two while continuing to squeeze your glutes.
tips: Keep the ribs down and the chin tucked — arching the lower back to get higher is the classic error.
Use a pad or towel on the bar; bare bar on the hips is genuinely painful.
Set the bench so it hits just under your shoulder blades.
barbell-hip-thrust.keyTip: Finish each rep with the hips fully extended and the glutes squeezed hard, with the ribs down — the top of the thrust is the entire point of the lift.

barbell-romanian-deadlift.name: Barbell Romanian Deadlift
instructions: Set up the bar in the rack to the level of your mid- thigh. You can also deadlift the bar off the floor up to the starting position.
Engage your lats and contract your abs. Take a deep breath in through your nose and start the descent by pushing your hips straight back.
Keep just a very slight bend at your knees and keep the bar as close to your body as possible, ideally right above the middle of your feet.

Keep your core braced and then exhale as you reverse the motion by pushing your hips forward while keeping the bar centered over your mid-foot. Once your legs are fully straight, repeat for another rep.
Spend about 2-3 seconds on slowly controlling the weight down, and then about 1 second to bring the weight back up.
To better engage the hamstrings, you can think about pulling the floor back with your heels as you come up.
tips: This is a hip hinge, not a squat — the knees stay mostly fixed and the hips move back.
Keep the bar dragging along your thighs; letting it drift forward loads the lower back.
Stop lowering when your back would round, not when the bar touches the floor.
barbell-romanian-deadlift.keyTip: Let the hips travel back until the hamstrings are fully stretched and stop there — depth is set by your hamstrings, not by the floor.

barbell-row-lat-focus.name: Barbell Row (lat focus)
instructions: Stand erect while holding a barbell with a supinated grip (palms facing up).
Bend your knees slightly and bring your torso forward, by bending at the waist, while keeping the back straight until it is almost parallel to the floor. Tip: Make sure that you keep the head.
While keeping the torso stationary, lift the barbell as you breathe out, keeping the elbows close to the body.
Slowly lower the weight again to the starting position as you inhale.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Tucked elbows and a low bar path are what bias the lats over the upper back.
Keep the neck neutral rather than looking up at a mirror.
Stop the set when your back rounds, not when your arms give out.
barbell-row-lat-focus.keyTip: Drive the elbows down and back towards your hip pockets — a lat-focused row lives in the elbow path, not in the amount of weight.

barbell-row-mid-upper-back.name: Barbell Row (mid/upper back)
instructions: Holding a barbell with a pronated grip (palms facing down), bend your knees slightly and bring your torso forward, by bending at the waist.
Now, while keeping the torso stationary, breathe out and lift the barbell to you. Keep the elbows close to the body.
Then inhale and slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Keep the spine neutral — rounding under a loaded row is where back injuries happen.
A more horizontal torso targets the mid and upper back; standing too upright turns it into a shrug.
Do not bounce the bar off your thighs or jerk with the hips.
barbell-row-mid-upper-back.keyTip: Pull towards your lower ribs with a flared elbow path and hold the squeeze for a beat — direction of pull is what makes this an upper-back row.

barbell-row-mid-upper-back-focused.name: Barbell Row (mid/upper back focused)
instructions: Holding a barbell with a pronated grip (palms facing down), bend your knees slightly and bring your torso forward, by bending at the waist.
Now, while keeping the torso stationary, breathe out and lift the barbell to you. Keep the elbows close to the body.
Then inhale and slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Keep the spine neutral — rounding under a loaded row is where back injuries happen.
A more horizontal torso targets the mid and upper back; standing too upright turns it into a shrug.
Do not bounce the bar off your thighs or jerk with the hips.
barbell-row-mid-upper-back-focused.keyTip: Pull towards your lower ribs with a flared elbow path and hold the squeeze for a beat — direction of pull is what makes this an upper-back row.

behind-body-cable-curls.name: Behind Body Cable Curls
instructions: Attach a handle to each cable and move it to the lowest position. Face away from the cable and grab the handle in each arm.
Take a couple small steps forward and let your arms hang straight slightly behind your body and towards the direction of the cable.
Brace your core, pull your shoulders down and away from your ears, and then while keeping your elbows locked in position, curl your hands up towards your shoulders.
As you do so, you should be curling up but also slightly inward to match the direction of the cable.
Once your arms reach roughly the level of your chest, control the weight back down until your arms fully straighten, and then repeat for another rep.
To perform this exercise one arm at a time, if you were curling your right arm for example.
tips: Keep the upper arm behind your torso the whole set — stepping back kills the point of the exercise.
Do not swing the torso to start the curl.
Cables keep tension at full extension, which a dumbbell loses.
behind-body-cable-curls.keyTip: Get a full stretch at the bottom of every rep with the arm behind your body — work done in the lengthened position drives the most growth.

bench-laying-sideways-lateral-raise-sing.name: Bench Laying Sideways Lateral Raise Single Arm
instructions: Lie down sideways on an incline bench press with a dumbbell in the hand. Make sure the shoulder is pressing against the incline bench.
Hold a dumbbell in your uppermost arm while keeping it extended in front of you parallel to the floor. This is your starting position.

While keeping the dumbbell parallel to the floor at all times, perform a lateral raise. Your arm should travel straight up until it is pointing at the ceiling. Tip: Exhale as you perform this movement..
While inhaling lower the weight across your body back into the starting position.
Repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
Switch arms and repeat the movement.
tips: Use noticeably less weight than a standing raise; the bottom range is much harder here.
Keep the torso still against the pad rather than rolling to help the arm up.
Keep the shoulder down and away from your ear.
bench-laying-sideways-lateral-raise-sing.keyTip: Lying sideways loads the side delt in the stretched bottom position that standing raises skip entirely — go light and use the full range.

bent-over-one-arm-row-dumbbell.name: Bent Over One Arm Row (Dumbbell)
instructions: Choose a flat bench and place a dumbbell on each side of it.
Place the right leg on top of the end of the bench, bend your torso forward from the waist until your upper body is parallel to the floor.
Use the left hand to pick up the dumbbell on the floor and hold the weight while keeping your lower back straight. The palm of the hand should be facing your torso. This will be.

Pull the resistance straight up to the side of your chest, keeping your upper arm close to your side and keeping the torso stationary. Breathe out as you perform this step. Tip: Concentrate on squeezing.
Lower the resistance straight down to the starting position. Breathe in as you perform this step.
Repeat the movement for the specified amount of repetitions.
tips: Keep your shoulders square to the floor — twisting the torso to finish the rep is momentum, not back work.
Row towards your hip, not your armpit, to keep the lat working.
Keep a neutral neck rather than looking forward.
bent-over-one-arm-row-dumbbell.keyTip: Let the dumbbell pull your shoulder blade down and forward at the bottom of each rep — the single-arm setup exists to give you that extra range.

bent-over-row-barbell.name: Bent Over Row (Barbell)
instructions: Holding a barbell with a pronated grip (palms facing down), bend your knees slightly and bring your torso forward, by bending at the waist.
Now, while keeping the torso stationary, breathe out and lift the barbell to you. Keep the elbows close to the body.
Then inhale and slowly lower the barbell back to the starting position.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Keep the spine neutral — rounding under a loaded row is where back injuries happen.
A more horizontal torso targets the mid and upper back; standing too upright turns it into a shrug.
Do not bounce the bar off your thighs or jerk with the hips.
bent-over-row-barbell.keyTip: Pull towards your lower ribs with a flared elbow path and hold the squeeze for a beat — direction of pull is what makes this an upper-back row.

bicep-curl-barbell.name: Bicep Curl (Barbell)
instructions: Stand up with your torso upright while holding a barbell at a shoulder-width grip. The palm of your hands should be facing forward.
While holding the upper arms stationary, curl the weights forward while contracting the biceps as you breathe out. Tip: Only the forearms should move.
Continue the movement until your biceps are fully contracted and the bar is at shoulder level. Hold the contracted position for a second and squeeze the biceps hard.
Slowly begin to bring the bar back to starting position as your breathe in.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Swinging with the hips and leaning back is the classic cheat — keep the ribs down.
Use an EZ bar if a straight bar bothers your wrists.
Do not let the elbows swing forward at the top to give the biceps a rest.
bicep-curl-barbell.keyTip: Straighten the arms completely between reps rather than stopping short — half-rep curls feel harder and build less.

bicep-curl-cable.name: Bicep Curl (Cable)
instructions: Stand up with your torso upright while holding a cable curl bar that is attached to a low pulley. Grab the cable bar at shoulder width.
While holding the upper arms stationary, curl the weights while contracting the biceps as you breathe out. Only the forearms should move. Continue the movement until your biceps are fully contracted.
Slowly begin to bring the curl bar back to starting position as your breathe in.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Do not lean back as the weight gets heavy.
Cables keep constant tension, so avoid resting at the top of the rep.
Keep the elbows fixed; letting them drift forward removes the load.
bicep-curl-cable.keyTip: Cables keep tension at full extension, so let the arms straighten completely at the end of every rep instead of stopping short.

bicep-curl-dumbbell.name: Bicep Curl (Dumbbell)
instructions: Stand up straight with a dumbbell in each hand at arm's length. Keep your elbows close to your torso.
Now, keeping the upper arms stationary, exhale and curl the weights while contracting your biceps. Continue to raise the weights until your biceps are fully contracted.
Then, inhale and slowly begin to lower the dumbbells back to the starting position.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Alternate arms or work both together — just do not use one to heave the other.
Keep the wrists neutral rather than curling them in at the top.
Control the lowering phase; that is where most of the work is.
bicep-curl-dumbbell.keyTip: Get a full stretch at the bottom of every rep — work done in the lengthened position drives the most growth.

bicep-curl-machine.name: Bicep Curl (Machine)
instructions: Adjust the seat to the appropriate height and make your weight selection. Place your upper arms against the pads and grasp the handles. This will be your starting position.
Perform the movement by flexing the elbow, pulling your lower arm towards your upper arm.
Pause at the top of the movement, and then slowly return the weight to the starting position.
Avoid returning the weight all the way to the stops until the set is complete to keep tension on the muscles being worked.
tips: If your elbows lift off the pad, the seat is too low.
Do not lean or shrug to move the weight.
The fixed path makes this safe to take to failure.
bicep-curl-machine.keyTip: Lower to near-full extension on every rep rather than stopping where the pad stops you — the stretched half of a curl is the productive half.

bulgarian-split-squat-glute-focus.name: Bulgarian Split Squat (glute focus)
instructions: Rest the top of your rear foot on a bench and take a long stride forward with the front foot.
Hold dumbbells at your sides, brace your core and hinge your torso slightly forward.
Lower under control until you feel a deep stretch in the front glute and the rear knee nears the floor.
Drive up through the front heel, squeezing the glute, then switch legs after the set.
tips: The long stance plus forward torso lean is what makes this glute-dominant.
Push through the heel rather than the toes.
Keep the hips square rather than letting the rear hip rotate open.
bulgarian-split-squat-glute-focus.keyTip: Take a long stride and lean the torso forward — the stretch you feel in the front glute at the bottom is the growth signal you are after.

bulgarian-split-squat-quad-focus.name: Bulgarian Split Squat (quad focus)
instructions: Stand a stride in front of a bench and rest the top of your rear foot on it, holding dumbbells at your sides.
Keep your front foot close enough that the shin can travel forward, torso mostly upright and core braced.
Lower straight down by bending the front knee until your rear knee nears the floor.
Drive up through the front foot, then complete the set and switch legs.
tips: A shorter stance and an upright torso bias the quads; a longer stance shifts work to the glutes.
Keep the front knee tracking over the foot rather than caving in.
Hold a rack with one hand if balance limits you before the legs do.
bulgarian-split-squat-quad-focus.keyTip: Keep the torso upright and let the front knee travel well past the toes — stance and torso angle decide whether this is a quad or a glute exercise.

cable-crossover.name: Cable Crossover
instructions: To get yourself into the starting position, place the pulleys on a high position (above your head), select the resistance to be used and hold the pulleys in each hand.
Step forward in front of an imaginary straight line between both pulleys while pulling your arms together in front of you. Your torso should have a small forward bend from the waist. This will be.
With a slight bend on your elbows in order to prevent stress at the biceps tendon, extend your arms to the side (straight out at both sides) in a wide arc until you feel a.
Return your arms back to the starting position as you breathe out. Make sure to use the same arc of motion used to lower the weights.
Hold for a second at the starting position and repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
tips: High pulleys bias the lower chest fibres; keep the path downward rather than straight in.
Keep the elbow angle locked and the shoulders down and back.
Do not let the stack pull you upright — stagger your feet and brace.
cable-crossover.keyTip: Cross your hands past each other at the finish so the pecs actually shorten fully — stopping at hands-apart leaves the squeeze on the table.

cable-lateral-raise.name: Cable Lateral Raise
instructions: Stand in the middle of two low pulleys that are opposite to each other and place a flat bench right behind you (in perpendicular fashion to you.
Now sit at the edge of the flat bench behind you with your feet placed in front of your knees.
Bend forward while keeping your back flat and rest your torso on the thighs.
Have someone give you the single handles attached to the pulleys. Grasp the left pulley with the right hand.
While keeping the arms stationary, raise the upper arms to the sides until they are parallel to the floor and at shoulder height. Exhale during the execution of this movement.
Slowly lower your arms to the starting position as you inhale.
tips: Keep the working shoulder down — shrugging turns this into a trap exercise.
Do not lean away from the stack to gain leverage.
Cables keep tension at the bottom where dumbbells lose it entirely.
cable-lateral-raise.keyTip: Start each rep with the cable pulling your arm across your body — that bottom tension is exactly what a dumbbell raise cannot provide.

cable-lateral-raises.name: Cable Lateral Raises
instructions: Attach a handle to the cable and move it to the bottom attachment. Face away from the cable and reach behind your body to grab the handle with one hand.
Take a couple steps forward and then a small step sideways towards the direction of your working arm.
Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Keep your arms just slightly bent and raise your arm diagonally at about 15 to 30 degrees in front of your body.
Raise until your arm reaches shoulder-height, control back down, and then repeat for more reps. Switch arms after you’ve rested for 30 seconds.
To perform two arms at a time, grab the left cable with your right hand and right cable with your left hand.
Turn so you face away from the cable and take a few steps forward. While keeping your arms just slightly bent, raise your arms into a wide Y position in front of you.
tips: Keep the working shoulder down — shrugging turns this into a trap exercise.
Do not lean away from the stack to gain leverage.
Cables keep tension at the bottom where dumbbells lose it entirely.
cable-lateral-raises.keyTip: Start each rep with the cable pulling your arm across your body — that bottom tension is exactly what a dumbbell raise cannot provide.

cable-pushdowns.name: Cable Pushdowns
instructions: Attach a rope attachment to a high pulley and grab with a neutral grip (palms facing each other).
Standing upright with the torso straight and a very small inclination forward, bring the upper arms close to your body.
Using the triceps, bring the rope down as you bring each side of the rope to the side of your thighs. At the end of the movement the arms are fully extended.
After holding for a second, at the contracted position, bring the rope slowly up to the starting point. Breathe in as you perform this step.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Elbows pinned to your sides — if they travel forward, you are turning it into a press.
Do not lean over the stack and use bodyweight to grind out reps.
With a rope, spread the ends apart at the bottom for a stronger contraction.
cable-pushdowns.keyTip: Lock your upper arms against your ribs so only the elbow moves — the moment the shoulder joins in, the triceps stop being the limiting factor.

cable-pushdowns-elbow-friendly.name: Cable Pushdowns (Elbow Friendly)
instructions: Set a pulley to the highest height. Use two rope attachments and pull them through so that the rope extends longer.
Grab one rope in each hand and take two to three steps back from the pulley. From here, with a slight bend at your knees, bend your torso forward about 30 degrees.
Bring your elbows down to your sides angled out just slightly and lock them there. Your hands should be around the level of your chest.
Brace your core, and then while keeping your elbows locked in place, use your triceps to extend your arms. You should feel as if you’re pulling the ropes down and out apart.
Keep your elbows locked as you control your hands back up to about the height of your chest, and then go down for another rep.
tips: Elbows pinned to your sides — if they travel forward, you are turning it into a press.
Do not lean over the stack and use bodyweight to grind out reps.
With a rope, spread the ends apart at the bottom for a stronger contraction.
cable-pushdowns-elbow-friendly.keyTip: Lock your upper arms against your ribs so only the elbow moves — the moment the shoulder joins in, the triceps stop being the limiting factor.

chest-dip-assisted.name: Chest Dip (Assisted)
instructions: For this exercise you will need access to parallel bars. To get yourself into the starting position, hold your body at arms length (arms locked) above the bars.
While breathing in, lower yourself slowly with your torso leaning forward around 30 degrees or so and your elbows flared out slightly until you feel a slight stretch in the chest.
Once you feel the stretch, use your chest to bring your body back to the starting position as you breathe out. Tip: Remember to squeeze the chest at the top of the movement for a.
Repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
tips: The forward lean is what makes it a chest dip; staying upright shifts the work to the triceps.
Stop at a stretch you can control — dropping into a deep dip is a common shoulder injury.
Use the assist or a band rather than cutting the range short.
chest-dip-assisted.keyTip: Hold the forward torso lean through every rep; standing tall quietly turns this into a triceps exercise instead of a chest one.

chest-fly.name: Chest Fly
instructions: Lie down on a flat bench with a dumbbell on each hand resting on top of your thighs. The palms of your hand will be facing each other.
Then using your thighs to help raise the dumbbells, lift the dumbbells one at a time so you can hold them in front of you at shoulder width with the palms of your hands facing.
With a slight bend on your elbows in order to prevent stress at the biceps tendon, lower your arms out at both sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch on your chest..
Return your arms back to the starting position as you squeeze your chest muscles and breathe out. Tip: Make sure to use the same arc of motion used to lower the weights.
Hold for a second at the contracted position and repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
tips: Keep the elbow angle constant — changing it turns a fly into a press.
Shoulders stay down and back, especially at the stretched position.
Moderate load, full range; this is an isolation movement.
chest-fly.keyTip: Slow the last third of the return and let the chest lengthen fully — the stretched half of a fly is where the stimulus is.

chest-press-machine.name: Chest Press (Machine)
instructions: Sit down on the Chest Press Machine and select the weight.
Step on the lever provided by the machine since it will help you to bring the handles forward so that you can grab the handles and fully extend the arms.
Grab the handles with a palms-down grip and lift your elbows so that your upper arms are parallel to the floor to the sides of your torso. Tip: Your forearms will be pointing forward since.
Now bring the handles back towards you as you breathe in.
Push the handles away from you as you flex your pecs and you breathe out. Hold the contraction for a second before going back to the starting position.
Repeat for the recommended amount of reps.
tips: If your shoulders roll forward at the bottom, you have gone too deep for your seat setting.
Keep elbows under the handles rather than flared high, which spares the shoulder joint.
The machine is stable, so it is a good place to push genuinely close to failure.
chest-press-machine.keyTip: Let the handles travel back until the chest is fully lengthened before pressing — the fixed path lets you chase that stretch safely.

chest-supported-machine-row.name: Chest Supported Machine Row
instructions: Load an appropriate weight onto the pins and adjust the seat height so that the handles are at chest level. Grasp the handles with either a neutral or pronated grip. This will be your starting.
Pull the handles towards your torso, retracting your shoulder blades as you flex the elbow.
Pause at the bottom of the motion, and then slowly return the handles to the starting position. For multiple repetitions.
tips: Keep your chest on the pad — pushing off it to move more weight is the usual cheat.
Lead with the elbows and think about the shoulder blades, not the hands.
Chest support makes this a safe place to push close to failure.
chest-supported-machine-row.keyTip: Because your torso is fixed, every extra rep comes from the back alone — let the arms fully straighten between reps and chase the stretch.

cross-cable-tricep-extensions.name: Cross Cable Tricep Extensions
instructions: Set two pulleys high and stand in the middle, taking the left handle in your right hand and vice versa.
Stand tall with arms crossed in front of your chest, elbows pointing down and pinned to your sides.
Extend both elbows, driving your hands down and out to your sides until your arms are straight.
Return under control until your forearms pass parallel, keeping the upper arms still.
tips: Keep the elbows fixed at your ribs — the crossed line of pull tempts the shoulders to help.
Stand square and brace so you are not being pulled to one side.
Squeeze hard at full extension; that is where this variation is hardest.
cross-cable-tricep-extensions.keyTip: The crossed line of pull loads the triceps hardest at lockout, so hold the fully extended position for a beat on every rep.

crunch.name: Crunch
instructions: Lie flat on your back with your feet flat on the ground, or resting on a bench with your knees bent at a 90 degree angle. If you are resting your feet on a bench.
Now place your hands lightly on either side of your head keeping your elbows in. Tip: Don't lock your fingers behind your head.
While pushing the small of your back down in the floor to better isolate your abdominal muscles, begin to roll your shoulders off the floor.
Continue to push down as hard as you can with your lower back as you contract your abdominals and exhale. Your shoulders should come up off the floor only about four inches.
After the one second contraction, begin to come down slowly again to the starting position as you inhale.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Do not pull on your head with your hands — that is a neck strain, not extra range.
Think of curling the spine rather than lifting the whole torso.
Exhale as you crunch to get a stronger contraction.
crunch.keyTip: Curl the ribcage towards the pelvis rather than hinging at the hips — spinal flexion, not sit-up height, is what trains the abs.

crunch-machine.name: Crunch (Machine)
instructions: Select a light resistance and sit down on the ab machine placing your feet under the pads provided.
At the same time, begin to lift the legs up as you crunch your upper torso. Breathe out as you perform this movement. Tip: Be sure to use a slow.
After a second pause, slowly return to the starting position as you breathe in.
Repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
tips: Move by flexing the spine, not by pushing with the arms or hips.
Keep the neck neutral rather than jutting the chin.
Exhale on the way down into the crunch.
crunch-machine.keyTip: Let the torso extend back until the abs are stretched before each rep — loaded ab work rewards range just like every other muscle.

cycling.name: Cycling
instructions: Set the saddle so your knee is only slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke.
Start with five minutes of easy spinning at low resistance to warm up.
Keep a cadence of roughly 80 to 90 revolutions per minute and adjust resistance to hit your target effort.
Hold that effort for your planned time, then spin easy for a few minutes to finish.
tips: A saddle that is too low is the most common cause of knee pain on a bike.
Keep the upper body relaxed rather than gripping the bars hard.
Push a cadence rather than grinding a huge gear at low revolutions.
cycling.keyTip: Set your saddle height first — a slight knee bend at the bottom of the stroke is worth more for both comfort and power than any resistance setting.

db-chest-supported-row-mid-upper-back.name: DB Chest Supported Row (mid/upper back)
instructions: Using a neutral grip, lean into an incline bench.
Take a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip, beginning with the arms straight. This will be your starting position.
Retract the shoulder blades and flex the elbows to row the dumbbells to your side.
Pause at the top of the motion, and then return to the starting position.
tips: Chest support removes the lower back and the cheating, so let the back do the work rather than heaving.
Lead with the elbows, not the hands — thinking about the hands turns it into a biceps curl.
Do not lift your chest off the pad to finish a rep.
db-chest-supported-row-mid-upper-back.keyTip: Let the shoulder blades travel forward at the bottom of each rep and pull them together at the top — the back grows from that full range, not from load.

dumbbell-chest-supported-row-mid-upper-b.name: Dumbbell Chest Supported Row (Mid/Upper Back Focused)
instructions: Set up an incline bench to an angle of about 30 degrees, typically the second notch up from the bottom.
Grab a pair of dumbbells using a thumbless grip and lay your chest on the bench with your arms hanging down by your sides and palms facing each other.
To stabilize your body, bring your shoulders down and away from your ears, squeeze your glutes and flex your abs.
Then, pull your elbows back behind your body at about a 45 to 60 degree angle away from your torso. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top position.
Control the weight back down to the starting position instead of letting it just drop. Let your shoulder blades open up, reset, and then go into your next rep.
Think about pulling with your elbows each rep in order to better activate your back.
tips: Chest support removes the lower back and the cheating, so let the back do the work rather than heaving.
Lead with the elbows, not the hands — thinking about the hands turns it into a biceps curl.
Do not lift your chest off the pad to finish a rep.
dumbbell-chest-supported-row-mid-upper-b.keyTip: Let the shoulder blades travel forward at the bottom of each rep and pull them together at the top — the back grows from that full range, not from load.

dumbbell-fly.name: Dumbbell Fly
instructions: Lie down on a flat bench with a dumbbell on each hand resting on top of your thighs. The palms of your hand will be facing each other.
Then using your thighs to help raise the dumbbells, lift the dumbbells one at a time so you can hold them in front of you at shoulder width with the palms of your hands facing.
With a slight bend on your elbows in order to prevent stress at the biceps tendon, lower your arms out at both sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch on your chest..
Return your arms back to the starting position as you squeeze your chest muscles and breathe out. Tip: Make sure to use the same arc of motion used to lower the weights.
Hold for a second at the contracted position and repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
tips: Keep the elbow bend fixed; bending more turns it into a clumsy press.
Use much less weight than you press — the leverage here is brutal on the shoulder.
Stop lowering when the stretch peaks, not when the dumbbells reach the floor.
dumbbell-fly.keyTip: Keep the soft elbow bend constant and stop at a strong but pain-free stretch — flyes reward range of motion, never load.

dumbbell-goblet-squat.name: Dumbbell Goblet Squat
instructions: Stand holding a light kettlebell by the horns close to your chest. This will be your starting position.
Squat down between your legs until your hamstrings are on your calves. Keep your chest and head up and your back straight.
At the bottom position, pause and use your elbows to push your knees out. Return to the starting position, and repeat for 10-20 repetitions.
tips: The front load naturally keeps your torso upright, which is why this is a good technique teacher.
Keep the weight tight to your chest rather than letting it drift forward.
Do not let the knees cave inwards on the way up.
dumbbell-goblet-squat.keyTip: Keep the weight pressed tight to your chest — the moment it drifts forward your torso follows and the squat stops being quad-focused.

dumbbell-lateral-raise.name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
instructions: Pick a couple of dumbbells and stand with a straight torso and the dumbbells by your side at arms length with the palms of the hand facing you. This will be your starting position.
While maintaining the torso in a stationary position (no swinging), lift the dumbbells to your side with a slight bend on the elbow.
Lower the dumbbells back down slowly to the starting position as you inhale.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Swinging with the hips is the most common error — if you have to heave it, go lighter.
Keep the shoulders down rather than shrugging the weight up with your traps.
Stop at shoulder height; going higher hands the work to the traps.
dumbbell-lateral-raise.keyTip: Control the lowering phase for two to three seconds — side delts respond far better to slow negatives than to heavier dumbbells.

dumbbell-lateral-raises.name: Dumbbell Lateral Raises
instructions: Grab a pair of dumbbells and stand with your feet about shoulder width apart and knees slightly bent. Lean your torso forward about 15 degrees.
Brace your core. While keeping your arms just slightly bent, raise your hands out in front of you. As you do so, raise your arms in a Y position in front of you.
This is about 15 to 30 degrees in front of your body.
Raise the weight until your arms reach shoulder-height, control them back down until your hands are down in front of your thighs, and then repeat for more reps.
To better help with muscle activation, you can try using a thumbless grip and rather than thinking about raising the weight up.
tips: Swinging with the hips is the most common error — if you have to heave it, go lighter.
Keep the shoulders down rather than shrugging the weight up with your traps.
Stop at shoulder height; going higher hands the work to the traps.
dumbbell-lateral-raises.keyTip: Control the lowering phase for two to three seconds — side delts respond far better to slow negatives than to heavier dumbbells.

dumbbell-lying-leg-curls.name: Dumbbell Lying Leg Curls
instructions: Lie face down on a flat bench with your knees just past the edge and a dumbbell held between your feet.
Press your hips into the bench and grip the bench for stability.
Curl your heels towards your glutes by bending the knees, squeezing the hamstrings.
Lower slowly until your legs are almost straight, keeping the dumbbell secure.
tips: Pinch the dumbbell firmly between the feet and keep the movement slow — a dropped dumbbell is the risk here.
Keep your hips pressed down rather than lifting them.
Start very light to get the foot grip right.
dumbbell-lying-leg-curls.keyTip: Keep the hips pinned to the bench and move slowly — with a dumbbell balanced on your feet, control matters more than the number of reps.

dumbbell-romanian-deadlift.name: Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift
instructions: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs, feet hip width and knees softly bent.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back with a neutral spine.
Push your hips back and hinge forward, keeping the dumbbells close to your legs.
Lower until you feel a deep hamstring stretch, then drive your hips forward to stand.
tips: Keep the knee angle fixed — bending and straightening turns this into a squat.
The dumbbells must track close to the legs, not swing forward.
Stop the descent when the lower back would start to round.
dumbbell-romanian-deadlift.keyTip: Keep the weights brushing your legs the whole way down; a dumbbell that drifts away from the body moves the load straight to your lower back.

elliptical.name: Elliptical
instructions: Step onto the pedals, take the moving handles and start at a low resistance to find your rhythm.
Stand tall with your whole foot on the pedal and your core lightly braced.
Push and pull with the handles while driving through the legs, keeping the motion smooth.
Build to your target resistance and hold it, then reduce resistance for a few minutes before stepping off.
tips: Coasting on momentum is easy here — keep resistance high enough that you are actually driving the pedals.
Do not hunch over the console or lean on the fixed rails.
Use the moving handles so the upper body contributes.
elliptical.keyTip: Set enough resistance that you have to drive each stride rather than letting the flywheel carry you — momentum is what makes elliptical sessions feel productive and not be.

face-pull-cable.name: Face Pull (Cable)
instructions: Attach a rope to a pulley set at roughly face height and step back with the rope in both hands, palms facing in.
Stand with a staggered stance, braced core and arms extended towards the stack.
Pull the rope towards your forehead, driving your elbows high and out and rotating your hands back.
Squeeze the rear delts and upper back, then return under control to a full stretch.
tips: Keep the elbows at or above shoulder height throughout, or it becomes a row.
Go light — this is a rear-delt and upper-back movement, not a strength lift.
Do not lean back to counterweight the stack.
face-pull-cable.keyTip: Finish each rep with the hands beside your ears and the elbows high; rotating back at the end is what makes this the best rear-delt cue there is.

flat-dumbbell-press.name: Flat Dumbbell Press
instructions: Grab a pair of dumbbells and sit on the edge of a flat bench.
Kick up the dumbbells one at a time as you lay back on the bench to get them into position with your arms straight over your shoulders.
Brace your core and then control the weight down by dropping your elbows to about a 45 to 60 degree angle from your torso. Allow your hands to naturally turn in slightly.
Continue lowering until the weights reach around the level of your torso, or as low as is comfortable for you.
Use your chest to push the weight back up until your arms are fully locked out and directly over your shoulders.
Think about pulling your arms together as if you were trying to touch your biceps together to move the weight up.
tips: Keep the shoulder blades retracted the whole set — letting them roll forward shifts load onto the front delt.
Flaring the elbows straight out to 90 degrees is the most common mistake and the hardest on the shoulder.
Do not clang the dumbbells together at the top; there is no tension there.
flat-dumbbell-press.keyTip: Lower until you feel a deep stretch across the chest before pressing — the bottom of the rep is where the growth stimulus lives.

flat-machine-chest-press.name: Flat Machine Chest Press
instructions: Sit down on the Chest Press Machine and select the weight.
Step on the lever provided by the machine since it will help you to bring the handles forward so that you can grab the handles and fully extend the arms.
Grab the handles with a palms-down grip and lift your elbows so that your upper arms are parallel to the floor to the sides of your torso. Tip: Your forearms will be pointing forward since.
Now bring the handles back towards you as you breathe in.
Push the handles away from you as you flex your pecs and you breathe out. Hold the contraction for a second before going back to the starting position.
Repeat for the recommended amount of reps.
tips: If your shoulders roll forward at the bottom, you have gone too deep for your seat setting.
Keep elbows under the handles rather than flared high, which spares the shoulder joint.
The machine is stable, so it is a good place to push genuinely close to failure.
flat-machine-chest-press.keyTip: Let the handles travel back until the chest is fully lengthened before pressing — the fixed path lets you chase that stretch safely.

flat-smith-machine-chest-press.name: Flat Smith Machine Chest Press
instructions: Place a flat bench underneath the smith machine. Now place the barbell at a height that you can reach when lying down.
As you breathe in, come down slowly until you feel the bar on your middle chest.
After a second pause, bring the bar back to the starting position as you breathe out and push the bar using your chest muscles. Lock your arms in the contracted position.
Repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
When you are done, lock the bar back in the rack.
tips: Bench position is everything on a Smith — if the bar touches your throat or belly, slide the bench.
The fixed bar path removes balance demands, so keep the weight honest and control the descent.
Set the safety stops at chest height before your first heavy set.
flat-smith-machine-chest-press.keyTip: Because the bar cannot drift, use that stability to pause briefly at chest level each rep and train the stretched position hard.

front-foot-elevated-reverse-lunges.name: Front Foot Elevated Reverse Lunges
instructions: Grab a pair of dumbbells and stand with your feet together on a small elevated platform like a weight plate. Brace your core.
While keeping your front leg planted on the platform, take a long step backwards with your other leg.
Keep your back neutral and lean your torso forward slightly by about 20 degrees to better engage the glutes. Continue descending until your back knee almost touches the ground.
Pause briefly in this position, and then push through the heel of your front leg to drive your hips forward, raising your body up back into the starting position with your feet together.
Avoid relying too much on your back leg to push your body up.
Instead, after taking your step back, think of your back leg as a kickstand for balance and don’t rely on it too much to kick yourself back up.
tips: The elevation increases the range of motion and the stretch on the front leg.
Keep the front heel planted on the platform throughout.
Hold something for balance if needed rather than cutting the depth.
front-foot-elevated-reverse-lunges.keyTip: The front platform is there to add depth, so lower until the rear knee is genuinely below the front foot's level and the glute is stretched.

front-raise-band.name: Front Raise (Band)
instructions: Pick a couple of dumbbells and stand with a straight torso and the dumbbells on front of your thighs at arms length with the palms of the hand facing your thighs. This will be your.
While maintaining the torso stationary (no swinging), lift the left dumbbell to the front with a slight bend on the elbow.
Now lower the dumbbell back down slowly to the starting position as you simultaneously lift the right dumbbell.
Continue alternating in this fashion until all of the recommended amount of repetitions have been performed for each arm.
tips: If your lower back arches to start the rep, the weight is too heavy.
Stop at shoulder height; higher recruits the traps rather than the front delt.
Front delts already work hard in every press, so keep the volume modest.
front-raise-band.keyTip: Stop the raise at shoulder height and lower slowly — the front delt already gets plenty of work from pressing, so quality beats load here.

front-raise-cable.name: Front Raise (Cable)
instructions: Pick a couple of dumbbells and stand with a straight torso and the dumbbells on front of your thighs at arms length with the palms of the hand facing your thighs. This will be your.
While maintaining the torso stationary (no swinging), lift the left dumbbell to the front with a slight bend on the elbow.
Now lower the dumbbell back down slowly to the starting position as you simultaneously lift the right dumbbell.
Continue alternating in this fashion until all of the recommended amount of repetitions have been performed for each arm.
tips: If your lower back arches to start the rep, the weight is too heavy.
Stop at shoulder height; higher recruits the traps rather than the front delt.
Front delts already work hard in every press, so keep the volume modest.
front-raise-cable.keyTip: Stop the raise at shoulder height and lower slowly — the front delt already gets plenty of work from pressing, so quality beats load here.

front-raise-dumbbell.name: Front Raise (Dumbbell)
instructions: Pick a couple of dumbbells and stand with a straight torso and the dumbbells on front of your thighs at arms length with the palms of the hand facing your thighs. This will be your.
While maintaining the torso stationary (no swinging), lift the left dumbbell to the front with a slight bend on the elbow.
Now lower the dumbbell back down slowly to the starting position as you simultaneously lift the right dumbbell.
Continue alternating in this fashion until all of the recommended amount of repetitions have been performed for each arm.
tips: If your lower back arches to start the rep, the weight is too heavy.
Stop at shoulder height; higher recruits the traps rather than the front delt.
Front delts already work hard in every press, so keep the volume modest.
front-raise-dumbbell.keyTip: Stop the raise at shoulder height and lower slowly — the front delt already gets plenty of work from pressing, so quality beats load here.

glute-focused-leg-press.name: Glute Focused Leg Press
instructions: Using a leg press machine, sit down on the machine and place your legs on the platform directly in front of you at a medium (shoulder width) foot stance. (Note: For the purposes of this.
Lower the safety bars holding the weighted platform in place and press the platform all the way up until your legs are fully extended in front of you. Tip: Make sure that you do not.
As you inhale, slowly lower the platform until your upper and lower legs make a 90-degree angle.
Pushing mainly with the heels of your feet and using the quadriceps go back to the starting position as you exhale.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions and ensure to lock the safety pins properly once you are done. You do not want that platform falling on you fully loaded.
tips: A high, wide foot placement increases hip flexion and so increases glute involvement.
Push through the heels rather than the toes.
Keep the lower back pinned to the pad throughout.
glute-focused-leg-press.keyTip: Push through your heels with the feet high on the platform — foot position is the only thing that makes a leg press glute-dominant.

hammer-curl-cable.name: Hammer Curl (Cable)
instructions: Stand up with your torso upright and a dumbbell on each hand being held at arms length. The elbows should be close to the torso.
The palms of the hands should be facing your torso. This will be your starting position.
Now, while holding your upper arm stationary, exhale and curl the weight forward while contracting the biceps. Continue to raise the weight until the biceps are fully contracted.
After the brief pause, inhale and slowly begin the lower the dumbbells back down to the starting position.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: The neutral grip targets the brachialis and brachioradialis, which add arm thickness.
Do not swing at the hips — if you need to, drop the weight.
Keep the wrists straight rather than letting them bend back.
hammer-curl-cable.keyTip: Keep the palms locked facing each other for the whole rep; rotating at the top quietly turns a hammer curl back into a standard curl.

hammer-curl-dumbbell.name: Hammer Curl (Dumbbell)
instructions: Stand up with your torso upright and a dumbbell on each hand being held at arms length. The elbows should be close to the torso.
The palms of the hands should be facing your torso. This will be your starting position.
Now, while holding your upper arm stationary, exhale and curl the weight forward while contracting the biceps. Continue to raise the weight until the biceps are fully contracted.
After the brief pause, inhale and slowly begin the lower the dumbbells back down to the starting position.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: The neutral grip targets the brachialis and brachioradialis, which add arm thickness.
Do not swing at the hips — if you need to, drop the weight.
Keep the wrists straight rather than letting them bend back.
hammer-curl-dumbbell.keyTip: Keep the palms locked facing each other for the whole rep; rotating at the top quietly turns a hammer curl back into a standard curl.

heel-elevated-goblet-squat.name: Heel Elevated Goblet Squat
instructions: Stand holding a light kettlebell by the horns close to your chest. This will be your starting position.
Squat down between your legs until your hamstrings are on your calves. Keep your chest and head up and your back straight.
At the bottom position, pause and use your elbows to push your knees out. Return to the starting position, and repeat for 10-20 repetitions.
tips: The heel elevation is there to let the knees travel forward, which loads the quads harder.
Stay upright; folding forward turns this back into a hip-dominant squat.
Keep the plate stable and the whole foot in contact with it.
heel-elevated-goblet-squat.keyTip: Let the knees travel far forward over the toes — the heel wedge exists specifically to create that deep, quad-biased knee flexion.

hiit-conditioning.name: HIIT / Conditioning
instructions: Warm up thoroughly for five to ten minutes with easy cardio and some light mobility work.
Perform your work interval at a hard but controlled effort, keeping technique intact throughout.
Rest or move easily for the prescribed recovery period so the next interval can be done at the same quality.
Repeat for your planned number of rounds, then cool down with several minutes of easy movement.
tips: If your output drops sharply each round, the intervals are too long or the rest is too short.
Keep hard intervals to two or three sessions a week — they cost real recovery.
Technique degrades under fatigue, so pick movements you can do well when tired.
hiit-conditioning.keyTip: Protect the rest periods as carefully as the work; a genuine interval session is defined by being able to repeat the same hard effort, not by never stopping.

hip-abductor-machine.name: Hip Abductor (Machine)
instructions: To begin, sit down on the abductor machine and select a weight you are comfortable with. When your legs are positioned properly.
Slowly press against the machine with your legs to move them away from each other while exhaling.

Feel the contraction for a second and begin to move your legs back to the starting position while breathing in. Note: Remember to keep your upper body stationary to prevent any injuries from occurring.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Leaning forward biases the upper glute; sitting upright targets the side of the hip more.
Do not slam the pads out — control both directions.
Pause at the widest point for a beat.
hip-abductor-machine.keyTip: Lean your torso slightly forward and pause at the outer position — that forward lean is what shifts this from hip flexor to glute medius work.

hyperextensions-back-hamstring.name: Hyperextensions (back/hamstring)
instructions: Lie face down on a hyperextension bench, tucking your ankles securely under the footpads.
Adjust the upper pad if possible so your upper thighs lie flat across the wide pad, leaving enough room for you to bend at the waist without any restriction.
With your body straight, cross your arms in front of you (my preference) or behind your head. This will be your starting position. Tip: You can also hold a weight plate for extra resistance in.
Start bending forward slowly at the waist as far as you can while keeping your back flat. Inhale as you perform this movement. Keep moving forward until you feel a nice stretch on the hamstrings.
Slowly raise your torso back to the initial position as you inhale. Tip: Avoid the temptation to arch your back past a straight line. Also.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Keeping the legs straight and the spine neutral biases the hamstrings and spinal erectors.
Do not arch past a straight body line at the top.
Move at the hips; a rounding and unrounding lower back is a different, riskier exercise.
hyperextensions-back-hamstring.keyTip: Keep the knees straight and hinge purely at the hips — that is what turns a back extension into a genuine hamstring and erector movement.

hyperextensions-back-hamstring-focused.name: Hyperextensions (Back/Hamstring Focused)
instructions: Using a back extension machine, adjust the thigh pads so that when you lay on it, the top of the pads are just below the crease of your hips.
Position your heels firmly against the foot pad and keep them planted as you perform the movement with your toes slightly pointed out.
Tuck your chin to align your neck with your spine and brace your core. From here, lift your chest up to extend your upper back.
Continue until your torso is in line with your lower body, or just slightly past it. Pause here for a second, and then reverse the motion to the starting position and repeat.
Once you master the exercise without weight, you can load it. One option is to use a barbell either empty or with light weight.
Grab the bar with a wider overhand grip about 1.5x shoulder width, and get into the starting position.
tips: Keeping the legs straight and the spine neutral biases the hamstrings and spinal erectors.
Do not arch past a straight body line at the top.
Move at the hips; a rounding and unrounding lower back is a different, riskier exercise.
hyperextensions-back-hamstring-focused.keyTip: Keep the knees straight and hinge purely at the hips — that is what turns a back extension into a genuine hamstring and erector movement.

hyperextensions-glute-focus.name: Hyperextensions (glute focus)
instructions: Lie face down on a hyperextension bench, tucking your ankles securely under the footpads.
Adjust the upper pad if possible so your upper thighs lie flat across the wide pad, leaving enough room for you to bend at the waist without any restriction.
With your body straight, cross your arms in front of you (my preference) or behind your head. This will be your starting position. Tip: You can also hold a weight plate for extra resistance in.
Start bending forward slowly at the waist as far as you can while keeping your back flat. Inhale as you perform this movement. Keep moving forward until you feel a nice stretch on the hamstrings.
Slowly raise your torso back to the initial position as you inhale. Tip: Avoid the temptation to arch your back past a straight line. Also.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Toes out and a tucked chin are the cues that shift this from lower back to glutes.
Do not arch hard at the top to feel a contraction; squeeze the glutes instead.
Keep the load modest so the glutes, not momentum, finish the rep.
hyperextensions-glute-focus.keyTip: Turn the toes out and finish by squeezing the glutes rather than arching the spine — glute focus comes from foot position and intent, not extra range.

incline-barbell-skullcrushers.name: Incline Barbell Skullcrushers
instructions: Lie on a flat bench with either an e-z bar (my preference) or a straight bar placed on the floor behind your head and your feet on the floor.
Grab the bar behind you, using a medium overhand (pronated) grip, and raise the bar in front of you at arms length. Tip: The arms should be perpendicular to the torso.
As you breathe in, slowly lower the weight until the bar lightly touches your forehead while keeping the upper arms and elbows stationary.
At that point, use the triceps to bring the weight back up to the starting position as you breathe out.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Angling the arms back keeps tension on the triceps at lockout instead of letting the elbows rest.
Use an EZ bar if a straight bar bothers your wrists or elbows.
Lower under control — the name is a warning, not a joke.
incline-barbell-skullcrushers.keyTip: Let the bar travel past your forehead towards the bench behind you; that extra few inches is where the long head actually gets loaded.

incline-bench-press-barbell.name: Incline Bench Press (Barbell)
instructions: Lie back on an incline bench. Using a medium-width grip (a grip that creates a 90-degree angle in the middle of the movement between the forearms and the upper arms).
As you breathe in, come down slowly until you feel the bar on you upper chest.
After a second pause, bring the bar back to the starting position as you breathe out and push the bar using your chest muscles. Lock your arms in the contracted position, squeeze your chest.
Repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
When you are done, place the bar back in the rack.
tips: Use a spotter or safety pins — an incline press is harder to bail out of than a flat one.
Keep your wrists stacked over your forearms to protect your wrists and elbows.
Do not let your hips rise off the bench to grind out a rep.
incline-bench-press-barbell.keyTip: Keep the incline shallow, around 30 degrees, and touch the upper chest each rep — depth and angle matter far more than the weight on the bar.

incline-bench-press-dumbbell.name: Incline Bench Press (Dumbbell)
instructions: Lie back on an incline bench with a dumbbell in each hand atop your thighs. The palms of your hands will be facing each other.
Then, using your thighs to help push the dumbbells up, lift the dumbbells one at a time so that you can hold them at shoulder width.
Once you have the dumbbells raised to shoulder width, rotate your wrists forward so that the palms of your hands are facing away from you. This will be your starting position.
Be sure to keep full control of the dumbbells at all times. Then breathe out and push the dumbbells up with your chest.
Lock your arms at the top, hold for a second, and then start slowly lowering the weight. Tip Ideally, lowering the weights should take about twice as long as raising them.
Repeat the movement for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
tips: Too steep an incline turns this into a shoulder press — 30 degrees is usually the sweet spot.
Keep your head and upper back on the pad rather than craning forward to watch the dumbbells.
Set the dumbbells down by bringing your knees up, never by dropping them behind you.
incline-bench-press-dumbbell.keyTip: The low incline is chosen to bias the upper chest — keep the elbows slightly tucked and chase depth, not a steeper bench angle.

incline-db-overhead-extensions.name: Incline DB Overhead Extensions
instructions: Sit down on a bench with back support and grasp a dumbbell with both hands and hold it overhead at arm's length. Tip: a better way is to have somebody hand it to you especially.

Keeping your upper arms close to your head (elbows in) and perpendicular to the floor, lower the resistance in a semi-circular motion behind your head until your forearms touch your biceps. Tip: The upper arms.
Go back to the starting position by using the triceps to raise the dumbbell. Breathe out as you perform this step.
Repeat for the recommended amount of repetitions.
tips: Keeping the arms overhead is the point — it puts the long head of the triceps on stretch.
Flaring the elbows is the usual cheat; keep them roughly shoulder width.
Start lighter than you expect and earn the range of motion.
incline-db-overhead-extensions.keyTip: Overhead is the only position that fully lengthens the long head of the triceps, so chase the deepest comfortable stretch rather than heavier dumbbells.

incline-dumbbell-curls.name: Incline Dumbbell Curls
instructions: Set up an incline bench to just a slight angle back of about 60 degrees, which is typically 2 to 3 notches down from the top position.
Grab a pair of dumbbells and lay your back on the bench with your arms hanging straight down by your sides with your palms facing in and your feet planted firmly on the ground.
Pull your shoulders down and away from your ears and brace your core. While keeping both of your elbows locked into place, curl the weight up towards your shoulders.
As you do so, rotate your palms so that they face up towards the ceiling at the top position.
Lower the weight back down to the starting position letting your wrists rotate back into a neutral position. Once your arms fully straighten, repeat for another rep.
tips: Do not let the elbows travel forward as you curl — the upper arm stays back.
Use less weight than a standing curl; the stretched start makes it much harder.
Keep the shoulder blades against the pad rather than rolling forward.
incline-dumbbell-curls.keyTip: Let the arms hang fully straight behind your torso at the bottom — the incline exists to load the biceps in that stretched position.

incline-dumbbell-overhead-extensions.name: Incline Dumbbell Overhead Extensions
instructions: Set up an adjustable bench to an incline of about 45 degrees, which is typically 2-3 notches up from the bottom position.
Grab a pair of dumbbells and lay your back onto the bench with your arms straight over your shoulders and palms facing in towards each other.
Brace your core, flatten your lower back against the bench, and then while keeping your arms straight, move them back until they are parallel with your torso and lock them in this position.
Keep your elbows locked and then bend your forearms back behind your head as far as you can.
Extend your forearms straight without moving your elbows to get back into the starting position and then repeat for more reps.
tips: Keeping the arms overhead is the point — it puts the long head of the triceps on stretch.
Flaring the elbows is the usual cheat; keep them roughly shoulder width.
Start lighter than you expect and earn the range of motion.
incline-dumbbell-overhead-extensions.keyTip: Overhead is the only position that fully lengthens the long head of the triceps, so chase the deepest comfortable stretch rather than heavier dumbbells.

incline-machine-chest-press.name: Incline Machine Chest Press
instructions: Load an appropriate weight onto the pins and adjust the seat for your height. The handles should be near the top of the pectorals at the beginning of the motion. Your chest.
Press the handles forward by extending through the elbow.
After a brief pause at the top, return the weight just above the start position, keeping tension on the muscles by not returning the weight to the stops until the set is complete.
tips: If your shoulders shrug on every rep, the seat is set too low for your torso.
Keep elbows below the line of your hands to keep the load on the chest.
Machines are stable — use that to train the last few hard reps safely.
incline-machine-chest-press.keyTip: Set the seat so the handles start at collarbone height; starting too low turns an upper-chest exercise back into a flat press.

incline-walking.name: Incline Walking
instructions: Step onto the treadmill, clip on the safety key and start at a flat, easy walking pace.
Raise the incline gradually to your target grade and settle into a speed you can hold for the whole session.
Stand tall with your shoulders back and let your arms swing naturally instead of gripping the handrails.
Keep your foot strike under your body and your breathing conversational.
Lower the incline for the last few minutes to cool down before stepping off.
tips: Holding the rails offloads a large part of the work and makes the calorie estimate wrong.
Keep the effort at a level where you could speak in short sentences.
Build incline before speed — steeper walking is easier on the joints than running.
incline-walking.keyTip: Let go of the handrails and raise the incline instead of the speed — grade is what turns a walk into real cardiovascular work without pounding your joints.

jump-rope.name: Jump Rope
instructions: Set the rope length so the handles reach roughly your armpits when you stand on the middle of the rope.
Stand tall with elbows close to your sides and turn the rope with your wrists, not your arms.
Make small jumps just high enough to clear the rope, landing softly on the balls of your feet.
Keep a steady rhythm for your interval, then rest and repeat as planned.
tips: Jumping too high is what makes people tire out in thirty seconds.
Turn the rope from the wrists; big arm circles waste energy.
Build up gradually — the calves and Achilles take the load here.
jump-rope.keyTip: Keep the jumps barely an inch off the floor and turn the rope from the wrists — efficiency, not height, is what lets you skip for minutes instead of seconds.

kneeling-one-arm-lat-pulldown.name: Kneeling One Arm Lat Pulldown
instructions: Select an appropriate weight and adjust the knee pad to help keep you down. Grasp the handle with a pronated grip. This will be your starting position.
Pull the handle down, squeezing your elbow to your side as you flex the elbow.
Pause at the bottom of the motion, and then slowly return the handle to the starting position.
For multiple repetitions, avoid completely returning the weight to keep tension on the muscles being worked.
tips: Do not rotate or lean away from the stack to move more weight.
Keep a braced core so only the working arm moves.
A single arm lets you get more range than a bar does.
kneeling-one-arm-lat-pulldown.keyTip: Reach the working shoulder all the way up at the start of each rep — the single-arm setup exists purely to buy that extra lat stretch.

lat-pulldown.name: Lat Pulldown
instructions: Adjust the height of the seat or knee pads so that your thighs are securely locked underneath, with your feet flat on the floor.
Set your weight then stand up and grab the bar with an overhand grip just outside shoulder-width apart. Sit back down with your thighs under the pads. Tilt your upper back just slightly backwards.
Pull your elbows down until the bar reaches the level of your chin. Control the weight back up until your arms are almost fully straight, and then repeat for another rep.
To better engage the back muscles, you can try using a thumbless grip and think about pulling with the elbows rather than with your hands.
tips: Lean back a little, not a lot — a big swing turns a pulldown into a row.
Pull to the chest, never behind the neck.
Let the shoulders rise at the top; locking them short-changes the stretch.
lat-pulldown.keyTip: Let your shoulder blades travel all the way up at the top of every rep — the fully lengthened lat is where a pulldown does its best work.

lat-pulldown-machine.name: Lat Pulldown (Machine)
instructions: Sit down on a pull-down machine with a wide bar attached to the top pulley. Make sure that you adjust the knee pad of the machine to fit your height. These pads will prevent your.
Grab the bar with the palms facing forward using the prescribed grip. Note on grips: For a wide grip.
As you have both arms extended in front of you holding the bar at the chosen grip width, bring your torso back around 30 degrees or so while creating a curvature on your lower back.
As you breathe out, bring the bar down until it touches your upper chest by drawing the shoulders and the upper arms down.
After a second at the contracted position squeezing your shoulder blades together, slowly raise the bar back to the starting position when your arms are fully extended.
Repeat this motion for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
tips: Lean back a little, not a lot — a big swing turns a pulldown into a row.
Pull to the chest, never behind the neck.
Let the shoulders rise at the top; locking them short-changes the stretch.
lat-pulldown-machine.keyTip: Let your shoulder blades travel all the way up at the top of every rep — the fully lengthened lat is where a pulldown does its best work.

lat-pulldown-single-arm.name: Lat Pulldown (Single Arm)
instructions: Select an appropriate weight and adjust the knee pad to help keep you down. Grasp the handle with a pronated grip. This will be your starting position.
Pull the handle down, squeezing your elbow to your side as you flex the elbow.
Pause at the bottom of the motion, and then slowly return the handle to the starting position.
For multiple repetitions, avoid completely returning the weight to keep tension on the muscles being worked.
tips: Do not rotate or lean away from the stack to move more weight.
Keep a braced core so only the working arm moves.
A single arm lets you get more range than a bar does.
lat-pulldown-single-arm.keyTip: Reach the working shoulder all the way up at the start of each rep — the single-arm setup exists purely to buy that extra lat stretch.

lat-pulldown-underhand-band.name: Lat Pulldown - Underhand (Band)
instructions: Sit down on a pull-down machine with a wide bar attached to the top pulley. Adjust the knee pad of the machine to fit your height. These pads will prevent your body from being raised.
Grab the pull-down bar with the palms facing your torso (a supinated grip). Make sure that the hands are placed closer than the shoulder width.
As you have both arms extended in front of you holding the bar at the chosen grip width, bring your torso back around 30 degrees or so while creating a curvature on your lower back.
As you breathe out, pull the bar down until it touches your upper chest by drawing the shoulders and the upper arms down.
After a second on the contracted position, while breathing in, slowly bring the bar back to the starting position when your arms are fully extended and the lats are fully stretched.
Repeat this motion for the prescribed amount of repetitions.
tips: The underhand grip lets the elbows tuck, which the lats like, but it also involves the biceps more.
